# Introduction
Thousands of blazes that have erupted in 2019 can be acrued to human activity, whether intentionally or accidental. A common reason is to clear land. Using fire is an inexpensive and fast way to prepare the ground for agriculture and plantations. The fires are also used to dispose of waste, especially in places with non-existent rubbish collection. Many fire hot spots also overlap with peatlands which are naturally wet ecosystems that become highly flammable when drained for plantation. With an exceptionally powerful El Nino this year, the fires can grow out of control rapidly, especially during prolonged dry spells. This has resulted in hazardous smoke spreading across Singapore. The smoke was then carried northwards by winds from the south, affecting neighbouring countries including Singapore. Transboundary haze pose significant environmental and public health threats to the region. With the haze-belching fires in  Sumatra driving Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) levels up, monitoring and predicting the magnitude of pollutants in the air across Singapore is critical for public health advisories (Rayda, 2026) (Mungcal et al., 2026). When PSI levels surge past unhealthy standards, citizens have to change their way of life: outdoor school activities and sports are suspended, public events are restricted and and are advised to stay indoors. 

## Literature Review 
Traditional air quality forecasting approaches such as Multiple Linear Regression mainly rely on linear assumptions and have long served as standard baseline for air quality (Abdullah et al., 2020). Conversely, Machine Learning techniques account for non-linear relationships and time-lagged variables. Machine Leaning modeling frameworks such as Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have started to emerge as a way to effectively predict air quality (Palanichamy et al., 2022). Futhermore, Spatial Autoregressive model such as Vector Autoregressive Exogenous systems and Spatial Autoregressive models can be used to model how pollutants diffuse across interconnected geographic locations. Thus, this project investigates several machine learning algorithms for forecasting haze levels in Singapore, ultimately providing relevant information to responsible parties which allows them to mitigate and plan precautionary measures. 

## Problem Statement 
The problem statement centers on the operational challenge faced by public health authorities, which is mitigating the reporting latency between smoke generated by Indonesia and public health advisories in Singapore. Without predictive tools, authorities risk reacting only after the haze has covered Singapore. Thus, this project aims to accurately forecast regional air quality pollution levels across Singapore before the haze covers the island, by leveraging on temporal dependencies and cross-station spatial patterns. By providing the framework, it would help provide crucial preparation time to issue public health advisories, distribute masks, which ultimately mitigates acute respiratory and cardiovascular health risks. 

# Data
The analyses uses 4 historical datasets compiled from official environmental monitoring networks and satellite remote sensing repositories. Regional air quality data which captures PM2.5 every hour, meteorological wind data which includes wind direction and wind speeds across Singapore are sourced from The National Environment Agency (NEA). Satellite fire hotspot data is obtained from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) fire archive. 

## Data Cleaning
Before analyzing, we cleaned the data to obtain a structured dataset. For satellite fire hotspot data, only those with a confidence score of 30% or higher were retained to eliminate false alarms. These fire records were then cleaned to only include the Sumatra region as the source based on their geographic coordinates. The records were aggregated daily to compute total Fire Radiative Power and cumulative fire counts. 

Meteorological wind data were cleaned by restricting the data to 5 representative monitoring stations in Singapore. Timestamps were standardized to uniform hourly blocks. To ensure wind dynamics could be interpreted linearly by the models, circular wind direction and wind speed were decomposed into orthogonal Cartesian velocity vectors. This gave East-West and North-South velocity components, where positive values represent winds from the South. 

Regional air quality data was filtered to only Southwest Monsoon haze window from 1 August to 31 October 2019. The hourly air quality data across all monitoring stations, hourly Cartesian wind vectors and daily Sumatra fire aggregates were merged based on the timestamps and dates. Since NASA FIRMS dataset only contains rows for days where a fire is detected, if a day has no fires, there will be no row for that date. Thus, when merging the datasets, any day without recorded fires will have a missing value. These missing values will be explicitly filled with 0, representing 0 fires on those dates.  

# Feature Engineering
Raw polar coordinates of wind speed and direction were transformed into Cartesian vector components (wind_u and wind_w) using trigonometric conversion:
$$
\begin{aligned}
u &= -\text{speed} \cdot \sin(\theta) \\
w &= -\text{speed} \cdot \cos(\theta)
\end{aligned}
$$
This isolates the North-South velocity component where positive values represent Southernn wind blowing northward. 

An interaction term was also engineered to model the physical interaction between the fire intensity and wind conditions. This means that Sumatra fire power only contributes to Singapore's pollution influx when southern winds blows northwards.
$$\text{smoke\_transport\_Sumatra} = \max(0, \text{wind}_w) \times \text{daily\_frp\_Sumatra}$$

# Methodologies 
## Elastic Net Regression (Baseline Regularized Model)
Elastic Net regularizes regression framework was implemented to forecast the West region's PSI levels at $t+1$ hour and $t+6$ hours, while handling multicollinearity among spatial monitoring stations. Elastic Net combines both Lasso and Ridge penalties to perform simultaneous variable selection and coefficient shrinkage. 

The feature space was constructed using temporal autoregressive lags across the 5 regional monitoring stations, spanning 0 to 5 hours and yielding 25 predictor variables. Prior to model fitting, all features were centered and scaled ($\text{preProcess} = c(\text{"scale"})$).

To prevent data leakage and simulate real-world forecasting performance during high-stakes pollution events, a strict chronological time-based split was enforced, utilizing August 1 to October 20, 2019 for training and October 21 to October 31, 2019 for out-of-sample testing. Hyperparameter tuning was conducted via 5-fold cross-validation over a grid of mixing parameters ($\alpha$) and penalty multipliers ($\lambda$). Out-of-sample forecasting accuracy across the test window was evaluated  using Mean Absolute Error (MAE).

## Random Forest
Linear models such as the elastic net cannot capture threshold effects, for example wind speed needing to exceed a critical value before smoke plumes reach Singapore. To account for such non-linear atmospheric interactions, we train a Random Forest (Breiman, 2001) of 500 trees to forecast the PSI level in the west region at two horizons: $t+1$ hour (immediate) and $t+6$ hours (extended). Predictors at time $t$ comprise the PSI of all five regions at lags 0 to 5 hours, wind vector components ($u$, $w$) and mean wind speed, and daily fire radiative power and hotspot counts for Sumatra, together with the Sumatra smoke-transport interaction term. Only Sumatra-based fire radiative power, hotspot counts, and smoke-transport features are included. The number of variables tried at each split (`mtry`) is selected by minimising the out-of-bag (OOB) mean squared error. The split is based on the forecast target timestamp: training targets run from 1 August to 20 October 2019, while the untouched test targets run from 21 to 31 October 2019. The same target-date windows are applied at both forecast horizons, and the Random Forest, Elastic Net comparison model and persistence benchmark are evaluated on the same test observations. Variable importance is measured by permutation: the percentage increase in OOB MSE when a predictor's values are randomly shuffled. Predictors are grouped into local (west) lags, other-region lags, wind, and Sumatra fire/smoke transport to assess whether local persistence or upstream inputs become more important as the horizon lengthens. Forecasts are compared using MAE.

## Support Vector Machine (SVM)
Following the kernel-comparison and tuning approach in Lab 6, we implement Support Vector Regression (SVR) using `caret` and `kernlab`. Unlike the lab's categorical response, the outcome is continuous West-region PM$_{2.5}$ at $t+1$ or $t+6$ hours. SVR fits a function that balances model complexity against deviations outside an epsilon-insensitive error band. Linear, polynomial and radial basis kernels allow us to compare a linear relationship with nonlinear alternatives.

The predictor set matches Phase 3: readings from all five regions at lags 0--5 hours, wind components and mean speed, Sumatra fire power and hotspot counts, and the smoke-transport interaction (36 inputs before removal of constant columns). Training targets fall before 21 October 2019, with the same 21--31 October test observations as Random Forest. Constant predictors are removed and the remaining inputs centred and scaled within each training fold.

We tune six linear configurations ($C=2^{-4},\ldots,2^1$), eight polynomial configurations ($C\in\{0.5,2\}$, scale $\in\{1/64,1/16\}$, degree $\in\{2,3\}$), and six radial configurations ($C\in\{0.5,2\}$, $\sigma\in\{1/16,1/8,1/4\}$). Three expanding chronological training windows precede seven-day validation blocks starting on 23 September, 1 October and 9 October. Training targets must precede each block's first forecast origin. The kernel and parameters with the lowest mean validation MAE are selected separately by horizon, refitted on all training data, and evaluated once on the untouched test set using MAE, RMSE and predictive $R^2$.

## VARX Spatio-Temporal Model
### Model Formulation
To model Singapore's five regional air quality series simultaneously rather than in isolation, we implement a Vector Autoregressive Exogenous ($\text{VARX}(p)$) system to capture inter-regional temporal dependencies across the island alongside external wind and fire conditions:

$$Y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} A_i Y_{t-i} + B X_t + \varepsilon_t$$

where:

* $Y_t = [\text{North}_t, \text{South}_t, \text{East}_t, \text{West}_t, \text{Central}_t]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^5$ is the endogenous vector of hourly regional $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ concentrations.
* $X_t = [\text{wind\_u}_t, \text{wind\_w}_t, \text{daily\_frp\_Sumatra}_t, \text{smoke\_transport\_Sumatra}_t]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^4$ is the exogenous vector capturing East-West and North-South wind velocity components, daily Sumatran Fire Radiative Power (FRP), and wind-driven smoke advection.
* $c$ is a $5 \times 1$ intercept vector, $A_i$ are $5 \times 5$ endogenous lag coefficient matrices capturing inter-regional diffusion, $B$ is a $5 \times 4$ exogenous impact matrix, and $\varepsilon_t$ is a vector white-noise innovation process.

### Stationarity Verification & Lag Order Selection
Valid VAR estimation requires all endogenous time series to be stationary so that parameter estimates remain consistent over time. Prior to fitting the model on the training set (August 1 – October 20, 2019; $n = 1,944$ hourly observations), we apply the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test to each regional series in $Y_{\text{train}}$. Next, we determine the optimal autoregressive lag order $p \in \{1, \dots, 10\}$ by minimising the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), balancing model fit against parameter complexity.

### Spatial Transmission & Diffusion Indicators
To test our physical advection hypothesis under the Southwest Monsoon, we conduct two diagnostics on the fitted $\text{VARX}(p)$ system:

1. Granger Causality Tests: We evaluate whether past $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ values in an upwind source region (specifically South and West) provide statistically significant predictive information for future $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ levels across the remaining regions beyond their own historical lags.
2. Impulse Response Functions (IRFs): Over a 24-hour window, we simulate a sudden $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ spike entering the South and West zones individually to trace how strongly and how quickly the smoke diffuses across the rest of the island.

### Out-of-Sample Forecast Evaluation
To ensure a direct and leak-free comparison against the other models in this study, we evaluate the fitted $\text{VARX}(p)$ system chronologically on the untouched holdout test window from October 21 to October 31, 2019. At each forecast origin $t$, we recursively generate multi-step predictions for both short-term ($t+1\text{ hr}$) and medium-term ($t+6\text{ hr}$) horizons using the estimated coefficient matrices $\hat{A}_1, \dots, \hat{A}_p$ and $\hat{B}$. Forecast accuracy on the West region is quantified using Mean Absolute Error ($\text{MAE}$).


## Spatial Autoregressive
The Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) model predicts PM$_{2.5}$ across Singapore's five regions at one and six hours ahead. It adds a relationship between neighbouring regions to a regression using current local pollution, wind components, Sumatra fire power and regional differences:

$$\mathbf{y}_{t+h}=\rho_h W\mathbf{y}_{t+h}+X_t\boldsymbol{\beta}_h+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t+h}.$$

The matrix $W$ defines fixed neighbour links. Central connects to all four outer regions, while each outer region connects to Central and two other outer regions. Linked neighbours receive equal weights that sum to one for each region. The same links are used at both horizons, with no hyperparameter tuning. The coefficient $\rho_h$ measures the strength of the spatial relationship and is estimated from the training data together with the regression coefficients using maximum likelihood. This method finds coefficient values that best explain the training observations.

Training targets run from August to 20 October 2019, and testing targets cover 21--31 October. The model calculates all five regional forecasts together without using their observed future pollution levels. Forecast accuracy is compared with OLS using the same inputs. West-region MAE is reported to match the other model comparisons.

# Results
## Elastic Net
Through 5-fold cross-validation, the model selected optimal tuning parameters of $\alpha = 0.5$ and $\lambda = 0.1$. This configuration reflects an even mixture of $L_1$ (Lasso) feature selection and $L_2$ (Ridge) coefficient shrinkage. The model achieved an out-of-sample Test MAE of 5.44 while the sparse coefficient matrix reveals that short-term pollutant persistence is heavily affected by immediate temporal proximity. Specifically, 1-hour historical lags have the strongest positive coefficients. Higher-order temporal lags (such as lags 3 to 5) were heavily shrunk or driven entirely to zero, indicating that immediate 1-hour momentum dictates short-horizon air quality states.
```{r enet-coef-t1, include = FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(Matrix)

best_lambda <- model_t1$bestTune$lambda
coef_mat_t1 <- as.matrix(coef(model_t1$finalModel, s = best_lambda))

coef_df_t1 <- data.frame(
  Feature = rownames(coef_mat_t1),
  Coefficient = round(coef_mat_t1[, 1], 4)
)
```

```{r enet-table-t1, echo=FALSE, results='asis',message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# This chunk has NO include=FALSE. It only outputs the kable table cleanly.
knitr::kable(
  coef_df_t1,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  col.names = c("Predictor Feature", "Coefficient"),
  caption = "Elastic Net Sparse Coefficient Estimates (t+1 Horizon)",
  align = c("l", "c")
)
cat("\n\\normalsize\n")

```

```{r enet-path-t1, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5, out.width="65%", fig.cap="Elastic Net Regularization Path and Coefficient Shrinkage across Penalty Parameter Lambda (t+1 Horizon)", fig.pos='H'}
# Directly plot the glmnet regularization path from the final model
plot(model_t1$finalModel, xvar = "lambda", label = FALSE)
```

At the multi-step 6-hour horizon, cross-validation selected $\alpha = 0$ and $\lambda = 1$. This parameter combination collapses the Elastic Net penalty into pure Ridge regression. The model achieved an out-of-sample Test MAE of 7.38. As expected, predicting further into the future leads to larger errors because unpredictable weather shifts accumulate over time. Unlike the sparse feature selection observed at $t+1$, the multi-step horizon benefited from retaining all 25 lagged predictors without aggressive feature zeroing. Since predicting PSI levels at $t+6$ hours requires capturing complex, island-wide weather patterns, retaining all past time data rather helps the model stay stable against sudden wind or weather changes.

## Random Forest 
 
### Forecast Accuracy at $t+1$ and $t+6$ Hours

The table below compares the Random Forest against an Elastic Net model and a persistence benchmark (forecast = current West PSI) on the held-out target period from 21 to 31 October 2019. For a like-for-like comparison, the Elastic Net is refitted in Phase 3 using the same predictors, training window and test window. Its figures may therefore differ from the Phase 2 Elastic Net baseline, which uses lagged PSI predictors only.

```{r rf-accuracy-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
phase3_metrics_report <- phase3_results %>%
  mutate(
    horizon = factor(horizon, levels = c("t+1 hr", "t+6 hr")),
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c("Persistence (naive)", "Elastic Net", "Random Forest")
    ),
    RMSE = round(RMSE, 2),
    MAE = round(MAE, 2),
    R2 = round(R2, 3)
  ) %>%
  arrange(horizon, model) %>%
  mutate(
    Horizon = as.character(horizon),
    Model = as.character(model)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(Horizon, Model, RMSE, MAE, R2)

phase3_best_t1 <- phase3_metrics_report %>%
  filter(Horizon == "t+1 hr") %>%
  slice_min(MAE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

phase3_best_t6 <- phase3_metrics_report %>%
  filter(Horizon == "t+6 hr") %>%
  slice_min(MAE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

knitr::kable(
  phase3_metrics_report,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  col.names = c("Horizon", "Model", "RMSE", "MAE", "$R^2$"),
  caption = "Phase 3 forecasting performance on the 21--31 October 2019 test window"
)
```

The table is generated from the Phase 3 model outputs whenever this report is knitted, so its values correspond to the current training and test split rather than values from an earlier run. At $t+1$ hour, **`r phase3_best_t1$Model[[1]]`** has the lowest MAE (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase3_best_t1$MAE[[1]])`). At $t+6$ hours, **`r phase3_best_t6$Model[[1]]`** has the lowest MAE (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase3_best_t6$MAE[[1]])`). The Random Forest's values should be compared with both benchmarks at each horizon; a lower test error indicates better out-of-sample accuracy.

![Random Forest forecasts vs actual west PSI on the test period](forecast_plot.png)

### Permutation Variable Importance

Permutation importance is computed separately at each horizon as the percentage increase in OOB MSE when a predictor is shuffled. Predictors are grouped into local (west) lags, other-region lags, wind, and Sumatra fire/smoke transport. Because the groups contain different numbers of variables, the table reports both each group's share of total positive permutation importance and its average importance per variable.

```{r rf-importance-group-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
phase3_group_report <- phase3_group %>%
  mutate(
    Share = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Average importance per variable` = round(avg_importance, 2)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(
  Horizon = horizon,
  Group = group,
  Share,
  `Average importance per variable`
)

knitr::kable(
  phase3_group_report,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "Random Forest permutation importance by predictor group"
)
```

![Share of permutation importance by predictor group](group_plot.png)

The group-level table and chart are recalculated from the current Random Forest fits. Compare the relative contributions across $t+1$ and $t+6$ hours to see whether recent PSI readings, wind, or Sumatra fire/smoke features gain importance as the forecast horizon lengthens. Importance is a measure of how much the fitted model relies on a predictor; it does not, by itself, establish a causal effect or guarantee better forecasting accuracy.

![Permutation importance of the top 15 predictors](importance_plot.png)

The top-15 chart ranks the predictors actually used by the fitted model at each horizon. The fire-related variables available to this Random Forest are `daily_frp_Sumatra`, `daily_count_Sumatra`, and `smoke_transport_Sumatra`. Any change in the ranking between horizons should therefore be interpreted in terms of the Sumatra fire and smoke-transport variables, wind conditions, and lagged regional PSI readings.

Daily Sumatra fire features are constant within a given day. This may limit how well the model generalises to later dates if it learns day-specific patterns rather than a stable relationship between upstream fire activity and Singapore PSI. The recalculated test-set metrics should be used to assess whether this limitation is reflected in the model's out-of-sample performance.

```{r svm-kernel-plot, echo=FALSE, out.width="85%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="Lowest mean chronological-validation MAE for each SVM kernel and forecast horizon.", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics("SVM_Kernel_Validation.png")
```

The linear kernel gives the lowest mean validation MAE at both horizons. Polynomial SVR is close at one hour (approximately 5.11 versus 5.09), but its six-hour validation MAE is higher (6.89 versus 6.63). The radial kernel performs less well within the tested grid. Thus, additional kernel flexibility does not improve validation accuracy in this experiment; this conclusion concerns the tested configurations rather than all possible nonlinear SVMs.

### Forecasts Versus Observations

```{r svm-forecast-plot, echo=FALSE, out.width="95%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="Selected SVM forecasts against West-region observations and the persistence benchmark at both horizons.", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics("SVM_Forecast_vs_Actual.png")
```

At one hour, the selected SVM broadly follows observed pollution fluctuations, but attenuates abrupt peaks around 23--24 October and sometimes predicts above the clean-air troughs. At six hours, forecasts are smoother and lag sudden increases, with larger errors around the major peaks on 23--24 and 29--31 October. Compared with the unadjusted persistence line, SVM reduces some delayed overshoots, although it still cannot reliably anticipate new pollution surges. The rise in test MAE from 4.51 to 6.85 is consistent with the reduced information supplied by current conditions at a longer horizon. Section 6.6 compares these West-region scores with the other models on the same target-date window.

These results are conditional on the tested kernel grids and three validation blocks. The six-hour cost lies at the lower end of the linear grid, so a wider search could select a different configuration. Although fold-specific scaling and chronological validation prevent future observations from entering model fitting, complete same-day fire aggregates may contain information unavailable at the forecast origin. The experiment therefore retains the retrospective information-availability limitation discussed for the other models.

## VARX Spatio-Temporal Model

### Stationarity and Optimal Lag Order
All five regional $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ training series yield Augmented Dickey-Fuller $p$-values below $0.01$, rejecting the null hypothesis of non-stationarity and confirming that the series are stable in levels without needing differencing. Minimising the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) identifies an optimal lag order of $p = 3$, indicating that regional air quality depends primarily on the preceding 3 hours of island-wide particulate levels alongside external wind and fire inputs.

### Directional Smoke Transmission (Granger Causality)
Both South and West regions yield highly significant Granger causality results ($p < 0.001$), proving that past $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ surges entering Singapore's southern and western boundaries statistically improve predictions of subsequent pollution across the rest of the island. Notably, North, East, and Central regions also return statistically significant $p$-values ($p < 0.001$), which reflects Singapore's small geographical size. This allows wind circulation to mix smoke across neighbouring zones within hours, resulting in a strong spatial interdependence that also directly motivates the Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) model explored in following sections.

### Impulse Response Function (IRF) Simulations
The 24-hour IRF simulations illustrate how a sudden smoke spike spreads across the island depending on the point of entry:

```{r varx-irf-plots, echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", fig.show="hold", out.width="49%", fig.cap="24-Hour Orthogonalized Impulse Response Functions for South (left) and West (right) $\\text{PM}_{2.5}$ Shocks", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics(c("VARX_South_IRF.png", "VARX_West_IRF.png"))
```

* South Shock Propagation: Following a sudden spike in the South, southern $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ peaks immediately ($h = 0$) before dissipating steadily over the next 15–20 hours. Across all other regions, responses climb rapidly and peak roughly 2 hours later, demonstrating rapid inland dispersion.
* West Shock Propagation: Following a sudden spike in the West, western $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ drops steeply within the first 2 hours before a small rebound after 4 hours, likely reflecting recirculated air feedback. As compared to a southern entry, the spillover peaks in other regions are smaller in magnitude and occur 4 hours post-shock. Geographically, the West region sits along the far western edge of the island, meaning smoke plumes entering from the west would require a longer transit window to reach other regions.

### Forecast Accuracy at $t+1$ and $t+6$ Hours
Across the October 21–31 window, the $\text{VARX}(3)$ model achieves an $\text{MAE}$ of $4.45\ \mu\text{g/m}^3$ at the $t+1\text{ hr}$ horizon, which increases to $6.86\ \mu\text{g/m}^3$ at the $t+6\text{ hr}$ horizon.

```{r varx-forecast-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.align="center", out.width="80%", fig.cap="VARX(3) Out-of-Sample $\\text{PM}_{2.5}$ Forecasts vs. Actual Observations for the West Region (October 21-31, 2019)", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics("VARX_Actual_Predicted_West.png")
```

Visually, the observed $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ levels demonstrate short-term volatility and fluctuate rapidly. In contrast, the VARX forecast generates a smoother trajectory that captures the broader overall trend from October 21 to October 31. At the $t+1\text{ hr}$ horizon, the model closely tracks the actual readings and successfully identifies most pollution build-ups. However, as the forecast horizon extends to $t+6\text{ hr}$, predictive accuracy reduces noticeably and the predicted line shows a clear lag behind sudden pollution spikes, such as on Oct 23-24. The model relies heavily on autoregressive historical lags, which means it cannot anticipate sudden spikes ahead of time. Consequently, the predictions only react hours later, after the elevated readings enter recent observed data.

Across both time horizons, the model also tends to underpredict the magnitude of extreme peaks while overestimating pollution levels when the air is relatively clean. Its predictions are overly smoothed as the linear VARX system minimises overall mean squared error. Despite these differences, the model generally follows the true trajectory especially at a shorter horizon.

## Spatial Autoregressive
### Forecast Accuracy

```{r sar-results-summary, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sar_report_t1 <- phase5_results %>% filter(Horizon == "t+1 hr", Model == "SAR")
sar_report_t6 <- phase5_results %>% filter(Horizon == "t+6 hr", Model == "SAR")
ols_report_t1 <- phase5_results %>% filter(Horizon == "t+1 hr", Model == "OLS")
ols_report_t6 <- phase5_results %>% filter(Horizon == "t+6 hr", Model == "OLS")
sar_mae_gain_t1 <- 100 * (ols_report_t1$MAE - sar_report_t1$MAE) / ols_report_t1$MAE
sar_mae_gain_t6 <- 100 * (ols_report_t6$MAE - sar_report_t6$MAE) / ols_report_t6$MAE
knitr::kable(
  phase5_results %>% dplyr::select(Horizon, Model, MAE),
  format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, position = "H",
  caption = "OLS and fixed-neighbour SAR test MAE for West, 21--31 October 2019"
)
```

Using the original fixed neighbour links, SAR achieves a test MAE of **`r sprintf("%.2f", sar_report_t1$MAE)`** at one hour and **`r sprintf("%.2f", sar_report_t6$MAE)`** at six hours. OLS gives **`r sprintf("%.2f", ols_report_t1$MAE)`** and **`r sprintf("%.2f", ols_report_t6$MAE)`**, respectively. SAR therefore makes slightly smaller average errors at both horizons. This suggests that including neighbouring regions helps prediction, although the improvement over OLS is small. Both models have larger errors when predicting six hours ahead.

### Forecasts Versus Observations

```{r sar-forecast-plot, echo=FALSE, out.width="95%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="SAR and OLS forecasts compared with actual West-region PM2.5.", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics("SAR_Forecast_vs_Actual.png")
```

At one hour, SAR follows most of the rises and falls in pollution. However, it still misses some sharp peaks, especially around 23--24 October. At six hours, predictions are smoother and often react late to sudden changes. The model tends to predict below the highest peaks and above the lowest readings. The SAR and OLS lines are close together, which agrees with their similar MAEs.

### Spatial Dependence

```{r sar-spatial-plot, echo=FALSE, out.width="85%", fig.align='center', fig.cap="Estimated spatial coefficients using the original fixed neighbour links.", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics("SAR_Spatial_Coefficient.png")
```

The estimated spatial coefficient is **`r sprintf("%.3f", phase5_spatial$rho[1])`** at one hour and **`r sprintf("%.3f", phase5_spatial$rho[2])`** at six hours. Both values are positive: after accounting for the other inputs, pollution levels in linked regions tend to move together. The six-hour model has a larger spatial coefficient, but also a larger forecasting error. A stronger spatial relationship therefore does not guarantee a more accurate forecast. These results show a statistical relationship between regions; they do not prove how much smoke physically travels between them.

## Model Evaluation and Comparison
```{r model-comparison-table, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, }
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)

# Helper function to extract MAE safely from your script's result data frames
extract_mae <- function(df, model_name, hor, model_col = "model", hor_col = "horizon") {
  res <- df %>% filter(.data[[model_col]] == model_name, .data[[hor_col]] == hor)
  if (nrow(res) > 0) {
    return(round(res$MAE[1], 2))
  } else {
    return("Pending")
  }
}

# Build the comparison table dynamically from your script's output objects
comparison_df <- data.frame(
  Model_Architecture = c(
    "Elastic Net (Linear Baseline)", 
    "Random Forest (Non-Linear Tree)", 
    "SVM (Support Vector Regression)",
    "VARX (Spatio-Temporal)", 
    "Spatial Autoregressive (SAR)"
  ),
  MAE_t1 = c(
    extract_mae(elastic_net_results, "Elastic Net", "t+1 hr"),
    extract_mae(phase3_results, "Random Forest", "t+1 hr"),
    extract_mae(svm_results, "SVM", "t+1 hr"),
    extract_mae(phase4_results, "VARX", "t+1 hr"),
    extract_mae(phase5_results, "SAR", "t+1 hr", model_col = "Model", hor_col = "Horizon")
  ),
  MAE_t6 = c(
    extract_mae(elastic_net_results, "Elastic Net", "t+6 hr"),
    extract_mae(phase3_results, "Random Forest", "t+6 hr"),
    extract_mae(svm_results, "SVM", "t+6 hr"),
    extract_mae(phase4_results, "VARX", "t+6 hr"),
    extract_mae(phase5_results, "SAR", "t+6 hr", model_col = "Model", hor_col = "Horizon")
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Render the publication-quality LaTeX table with dynamic cross-referencing
knitr::kable(
  comparison_df,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  col.names = c("Model Architecture", "Test MAE (t+1)", "Test MAE (t+6)"),
  caption = "Out-of-Sample Forecasting Performance Comparison Across All Model Architectures (Test MAE in $\\mu\\text{g/m}^3$)",
  align = c("l", "c", "c")
)
```
Table \ref{tab:model-comparison-table} summarises the out-of-sample Test MAE for the West region across all five models over the 21-31 October 2019 holdout window. At the $t+1\text{ hr}$ horizon, SAR records the lowest MAE (`r sprintf("%.2f", sar_report_t1$MAE)` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$), closely followed by VARX(3) (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase4_results$MAE[phase4_results$horizon == "t+1 hr"])` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$) and linear SVM (`r sprintf("%.2f", svm_report_t1$MAE)` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$). In contrast, the non-linear Random Forest (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase3_results$MAE[phase3_results$model == "Random Forest" & phase3_results$horizon == "t+1 hr"])` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$) and baseline Elastic Net (`r sprintf("%.2f", elastic_net_results$MAE[elastic_net_results$horizon == "t+1 hr"])` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$) yield higher short-term errors.

At the $t+6\text{ hr}$ horizon, MAE increases across all model architectures as longer gaps allow unpredictable weather changes to build up over time. SVM (`r sprintf("%.2f", svm_report_t6$MAE)` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$) and VARX(3) (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase4_results$MAE[phase4_results$horizon == "t+6 hr"])` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$) maintain the lowest MAE, outperforming SAR (`r sprintf("%.2f", sar_report_t6$MAE)` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$), Elastic Net (`r sprintf("%.2f", elastic_net_results$MAE[elastic_net_results$horizon == "t+6 hr"])` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$), and Random Forest (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase3_results$MAE[phase3_results$model == "Random Forest" & phase3_results$horizon == "t+6 hr"])` $\mu\text{g/m}^3$).

\clearpage
# Discussion

## Key Findings
**Forecast performance depends on the prediction horizon.** Among the five implementations in Section 6.6, SAR has the lowest one-hour West-region MAE (`r sprintf("%.2f", sar_report_t1$MAE)`), followed by VARX (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase4_results$MAE[phase4_results$horizon == "t+1 hr"])`) and SVM (`r sprintf("%.2f", svm_report_t1$MAE)`). At six hours, SVM (`r sprintf("%.2f", svm_report_t6$MAE)`) and VARX (`r sprintf("%.2f", phase4_results$MAE[phase4_results$horizon == "t+6 hr"])`) give the lowest point estimates. Their approximately 0.01 difference is insufficient to establish a meaningful advantage without uncertainty analysis. No single model is best at both horizons.

**Recent pollution readings are informative, but abrupt changes remain difficult to anticipate.** MAE increases from one to six hours for every model in the comparison. Elastic Net's coefficient analysis highlights the contribution of recent regional readings, while the forecast plots show increasing smoothing, delayed responses and missed peaks at the longer horizon. These patterns support short-term forecasting from observed pollution history, but indicate that six-hour forecasts provide less reliable information about the timing and magnitude of sudden surges.

**Additional nonlinear flexibility does not automatically improve generalisation.** Validation selects linear SVMs over the tested polynomial and radial alternatives at both horizons. Random Forest records MAEs of 5.53 and 8.58, exceeding the persistence benchmark's 4.56 and 7.70, respectively; it also underperforms the matched Phase 3 Elastic Net. The Phase 2 Elastic Net baseline achieves 5.44 and 7.38. Together, these results favour carefully regularised or structured models over assuming that a more flexible model will perform better. Different predictor sets and tuning procedures mean that the overall ranking describes these fitted implementations rather than an isolated effect of model architecture.

**Spatial information contributes predictive value, while environmental importance varies with horizon.** SAR has slightly lower MAE than OLS at both horizons when using the same inputs and fixed neighbour links. Positive rho estimates and VARX's regional predictive relationships support modelling dependence across Singapore. Random Forest assigns the largest aggregate importance share to other-region lags, although that group contains more predictors. Wind and fire/smoke importance shares increase at six hours, suggesting greater model reliance on environmental inputs as local persistence weakens. These associations and model-based IRFs do not by themselves prove physical smoke transport. Findings remain specific to the 2019 holdout period and retrospective daily fire features, so operational use requires further time-based validation with inputs available at each forecast origin.

## Limitations and Future Work 
* Daily Fire Data Aggregates: NASA FIRMS hotspot counts and Fire Radiative Power (`daily_frp_Sumatra`) are aggregated daily and remain constant across the whole day. In a real-time operational setting, complete end-of-day satellite fire totals are not yet available during earlier hours of the day, introducing look-ahead bias. Future implementations should filter satellite fire records by their exact detection time (`acq_time`) so that only fires observed before hour $t$ are included as predictors.
* Use of Future Wind Data in Multi-Step Forecasts: Multi-step forecasts at $t+6\text{ hr}$ in the VARX model utilise observed wind vectors (`wind_u`, `wind_w`) across the forecast window rather than values from weather forecasts. In real life, operational predictions would require integrating hourly forecasted wind fields from meteorological agencies to prevent error inflation during sudden wind shifts.
* Single-Season Evaluation Window: All models were trained and tested exclusively on the August–October 2019 haze episode, with evaluation limited to a single holdout window (21–31 October 2019). Validating across multiple haze episodes (such as 2015 and 2023) would better test whether our model accuracy holds under different weather and fire intensities.
* Smoothing of Extreme Peaks: All five models treat under-predicting and over-predicting pollution equally since they all minimise symmetric error metrics. Asymmetric loss functions can be applied instead to penalise missed hazardous alerts more heavily than false alarms.
* Single-Point Forecast Constraints: The current models output single-point predictions without indicating forecast uncertainty. Future work could generate prediction intervals (e.g., Quantile Regression, Conformal Prediction) to provide public health authorities with upper-bound risk alerts.
